title: Quadratic Sample Complexity for Strictly Replicable Realizable Learning with Unknown Marginals
summary: Under the quantifier $\exists A\,\forall D$, where the realizable distribution and its marginal are unknown, we determine the finite-class sample-complexity exponent for strict replicability: two independent samples and one shared seed must produce identical functions. For $\varepsilon=δ=ρ=10^{-4}$, the worst case over $|H|\le M$ is $Θ((\log M)^2)$, without iterated logarithms. For $d\ge1$, $0<\varepsilon\le1/16$, and $0<δ,ρ\le10^{-3}$, every randomized, possibly improper learner valid throughout an explicit anchored realizable family requires $Ω(d^2/(\varepsilonρ^2))$ samples. For the full Boolean class $P_d$, $d\ge2$, in the same parameter range, we prove the matching characterization $Θ(d^2/(\varepsilonρ^2)+\varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/δ))$ using a proper Poissonized ball-sampling algorithm. We also give an explicit proper Gibbs upper bound for every finite measurable Boolean class. Our lower bound uses square-root probabilities and volumetric packing; the Gibbs proof builds on established coupling and generalization identities. Finally, we characterize the known-marginal worst case for $P_d$, showing why that interface must be kept distinct.

title: Dynamic Dual-Feedback Conformal Inference for Time Series Forecasting
summary: Quantifying uncertainty in time series forecasting is particularly demanding because sequential data exhibit temporal dependence and are prone to distributional changes. Conformal inference has emerged as a powerful uncertainty quantification approach through the construction of prediction sets. Recent advances have introduced online conformal methods that adaptively adjust prediction thresholds through feedback mechanisms. However, the existing feedback mechanism typically relies solely on miscoverage indicators (actual feedback), whether the true label falls within the interval at each time step, while overlooking the empirical prediction threshold (estimated feedback) that is derived from the oracle conformal method. In this paper, we propose Dynamic Dual-feedback Conformal Inference (DDCI), which incorporates a dual-feedback mechanism consisting of actual feedback and estimated feedback. The former drives the primary adjustment of the intervals based on true observations, while the latter dampens excessive expansions or contractions by leveraging empirical thresholds from conformal inference during updates. By balancing these two signals, DDCI achieves more stable and narrower prediction intervals in sequential settings while maintaining near-nominal coverage in practice.

title: Robust Latent Variable Graphical Models: Exact Recovery and Fundamental Limits
summary: We study robust estimation of a Gaussian precision matrix that decomposes as a sparse matrix minus a symmetric, possibly indefinite, low-rank matrix, a structure that arises when latent-variable marginalization is combined with conditioning on linear measurements. The proposed convex estimator replaces the sample covariance by the centered Gaussian measure-transformed (MT) covariance, which preserves the signed graph of the sparse component under the nominal model, and penalizes the low-rank component by the nuclear norm of a congruence transform, an atomic norm that encodes structural side information. Our main result is a primal--dual witness theorem: under restricted invertibility and irrepresentability conditions on the Fisher information, the raw convex optimizer is unique, has no false edges, recovers the signs of all sufficiently strong edges, and has exactly the true rank and inertia. These conditions reduce to the graphical-lasso conditions when the low-rank part is absent, and we verify them from primitive incoherence and near-isotropy assumptions. Over a class on which they hold uniformly, we prove information-theoretic limits for Frobenius estimation, signed graph recovery, and inertia recovery. In particular, inertia recovery requires $N\gtrsim p/ν_{\min}^2$ samples, where $ν_{\min}$ is the smallest nonzero eigenvalue modulus of the low-rank part; the spectral beta-min condition of the witness theorem is necessary up to a $\sqrt{\log p}$ factor; and the Frobenius risk attains the minimax rate up to a factor $\sqrt{μ(1+\min\{d,r\})\log p}$, where $μ$ is the incoherence parameter, $d$ the maximal degree, and $r$ the rank. We further quantify robustness under Huber contamination, with a bias bound that is sharp for the MT functional and vanishes for remote outliers, and give a globally convergent linearized ADMM with closed-form updates.

title: H2DF: Calibrated Target Bands for Controllable Language-Model Unlearning
summary: Gradient ascent (GA) is a simple language-model unlearning baseline, but it continues increasing forget loss after useful forgetting has occurred. This unbounded pressure can damage retained utility and make forgotten examples abnormally high-loss. We introduce H2DF, a calibrated target-band objective that applies GA-like pressure below a data-dependent lower target and suppresses, or reverses, that pressure after the target region is reached. The targets are estimated from matched non-member examples before training, so the base objective requires one forget-batch forward/backward pass per optimization step; our reported TOFU variant adds sparse retain replay every tenth step. We instantiate a one-sided objective for TOFU question answering and a two-sided objective for MUSE-News language modeling. Across three TOFU seeds, H2DF obtains a forget NLL of 1.528 with margin 0.049 and retain NLL of 1.165 with margin 0.047, matching GradDiff while using retain replay only every tenth step and showing substantially lower variability than GA. On MUSE-News, H2DF improves retention over GA and NPO and is competitive with SimNPO, but does not dominate it. Ablations show that the upper target reduces overshoot and that validation-based checkpoint selection is important. These results support calibrated target bands as a practical mechanism for controlling forgetting strength, while also exposing sensitivity to random seed and calibration quality.

title: Atlas of MICCAI: 28 Years of Representation, Collaboration, and the Road to Inclusion
summary: Scientific knowledge in medical image analysis is shaped by venues such as the Medical Image Computing and Computer-Assisted Intervention (MICCAI) conference, which influence research agendas, professional credibility, and access to opportunity. As AI methods increasingly depend on large-scale data and compute, these dynamics risk further concentrating influence within already well-resourced regions and institutions. Prior meta-research on MICCAI has examined reproducibility, evaluation, and citation practices, but offers limited insight into who participates in and shapes the field. To better understand these dynamics, we conduct a longitudinal bibliometric analysis of the geographic and institutional structure of the MICCAI community, drawing on 9,748 papers published between 1998 and 2025. We find that the USA and China together account for nearly half of all publications, that high-income countries dominate collaboration networks as central and bridging nodes, while lower-income countries remain peripheral, and that participation inequality (Gini index 0.86-0.91 among contributing countries) has declined only marginally over 28 years. We further analyze the evolution of research topics between 2021 and 2025, distinguishing stable core pillars (e.g., segmentation, diagnosis, MRI/CT) from emerging paradigms (e.g., foundation models), and identify a persistent long tail of underexplored application-method and organ-modality intersections. To support transparency and reproducibility, we introduce the Atlas of MICCAI dataset and an interactive dashboard. We contextualize these findings within existing MICCAI equity initiatives, and propose actionable recommendations to reduce participation barriers, build research capacity, and recognize a wider range of scientific contributions.

title: AutoTerm-SST: Adaptive Terminology Memory with Zero Session-Time Setup for Streaming Speech Translation
comment: Submitted to EMNLP 2026 System Demonstrations. Code available at https://github.com/luojiaxuan/autoterm-sst
summary: Retrieval-augmented speech translation improves rare terminology, but systems such as RASST still assume that users provide a glossary before each session. That assumption is inconvenient for live talks, while merging every domain into one growing glossary eventually places too many irrelevant terms in the same retrieval and prompt competition. We present AutoTerm-SST, an interactive system that removes session-time glossary upload and domain selection. It organizes a large offline terminology catalog into topic slices, matches recent streaming translation context to bilingual slice prototypes, and activates a compact multi-slice working set under fixed retrieval and prompt budgets. On five ACL and five ESO oncology talks, AutoTerm matches a known-domain reference in terminology accuracy (88.3% vs. 88.1%) and mWER-resegmented BLEU (45.09 vs. 45.19), while requiring no domain input. Compared with a one-million-entry merged glossary, it improves terminology accuracy by 3.9 points and BLEU by 2.30. Routing plus four-slice retrieval remains lightweight: the complete system runs at 0.406 RTF, and the vLLM host sustains 32 real-time sessions. The live demo exposes active slices and retrieved terminology as the topic changes, providing zero-setup terminology-aware streaming translation.

title: High-dimensional layer-state trajectories reveal the internal dynamics of transformer inference
comment: Expanded preprint with 17 main figures and 13 supplementary figures. Source data and code are archived on Zenodo
summary: Mechanistic studies of large language models localize function in parameters, attention heads or neurons, but those parts do not specify how one inference unfolds. We treat the ordered layer-state trajectory as the empirical process and test whether layer order defines a measurable computation. Across representative Qwen, Llama and Gemma checkpoints, realized order produced paths 1.60--2.24 times as aligned with their endpoint chord as endpoint-preserving shuffles. The order effect transferred to a lexical task, but was stronger in three random initializations of the same Qwen architecture, identifying an architecture-compatible scaffold rather than a training-specific law. Direct hidden states provided stronger mechanism coordinates than vocabulary readbacks, and a task-defined coordinate made candidate competition computable. After additive interventions failed, local transition actuators selectively controlled internal trajectories across checkpoints. A confidence gate then drove 17 of 87 held-out Qwen closure trajectories across the full-vocabulary top-1 candidate boundary while leaving all 203 non-closure top-1 outputs unchanged. Safety-matched action reassignment performed similarly, locating the gain in selective gating and the bounded actuator family rather than fine-grained dose assignment. Layer order exposes an observable, computable and behaviourally consequential process of transformer inference without establishing a complete theory of LLM dynamics or control of answer correctness.

title: Disentangling Depression from Cognitive Decline in Elderly Speech Using Concurrent Clinical Assessments
summary: Detecting depression from speech in elderly patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is complicated by overlapping acoustic effects of cognitive decline. Without disentangling these, classifiers risk learning cognitive rather than depression-specific patterns. We present a Korean elderly speech corpus of 89 MCI speakers collected over three years with concurrent depression (SGDS) and cognitive (MMSE) assessments. Both linear mixed-effects models and partial correlations identify the same pattern: of seven feature groups, only formant features are associated with depression after controlling for cognitive function, while widely used F0 features carry no signal. The F1+F2 subset achieves UAR 0.760 with just 12 features, outperforming both the full eGeMAPS baseline and self-supervised representations. These findings show that concurrent clinical assessments can identify interpretable, depression-specific acoustic markers in populations where cognitive and affective symptoms co-occur.

title: Positive, monotone, and convex Gaussian process regression with Laplacian eigenfunctions
summary: We study how to condition an existing Hilbert space Gaussian process (HSGP) expansion on positivity, monotonicity, or convexity throughout an interval. The expansion has Gaussian coefficients whose variances are given by the kernel's spectral density. At fixed covariance and noise parameters, we retain this coefficient law and represent each complete interval event as a threshold on one coefficient. Integrating out that coefficient gives a strongly log-concave marginal posterior with a normal survival weight, while conditional truncated normal sampling recovers the full constrained law. The construction also covers joint restrictions within the finite expansion. For individual restrictions, we characterize the thresholds through polynomial equations and bound posterior error from conservative numerical evaluation in total variation. Under spectral regularity, the conditioned finite posteriors converge in quadratic Wasserstein distance to the corresponding conditioned underlying GP posteriors as the computational interval expands and higher frequencies are retained. This convergence controls uniform discrepancies in the response and derivatives through the constrained order. Mercury lidar and leaf light-response applications illustrate the consequences for derivative inference.

title: WaveCommitments: Private and Verifiable Speech-Agent Marketplaces
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, under review for a conference
summary: Modern speech systems are evolving into ecosystems of autonomous speech agents that speak together, negotiate, and trade assets such as embeddings, spectrograms, or raw data. In such markets, sellers cannot reveal assets for evaluation due to privacy constraints, and buyers cannot price what they cannot test. Thus, we open-source WaveCommitments, an end-to-end design that pairs confidential asset valuation via Data Shapley inside a trusted execution environment with multivariate polynomial commitments. It enables selective openings and tamper-evident provenance to prove that a delivered asset matches the valuation while hiding everything else. Our extensive experiments across three known datasets and various tasks with state-of-the-art encoders, including Whisper, reveal that we speed up the best benchmarks by up to 20x while reducing their proof sizes by up to 39x. We also systematically study how a speaker's value shifts across tasks and encoders, revealing agent-level market prices.

title: PW-Pruning: Phase-Aware Expert Selection for Speech-Centric Omni-Modal Models
summary: Sparse routing reduces per-token computation but leaves the full expert bank resident in memory. We study expert pruning for speech-centric omni-modal models, where pooling calibration statistics can obscure the different expert demands of acoustic-input processing and text-answer generation. We propose PW-Pruning, a phase-aware extension of DO-ACP that constructs separate importance-weighted kernels for acoustic-prefill and teacher-forced answer tokens, then combines phase-weighted log-determinant marginal gains to select one static expert bank. On Qwen3-Omni, retaining 32 of 128 experts per layer improves MMAU-mini and MMSU accuracy over matched pooled selection by 3.20 and 4.38 percentage points, respectively, after supervised fine-tuning, averaged over three runs. Single-phase and shuffled-label controls on this public backbone suggest that semantic phase information contributes to these gains. Experiments on a non-public Qwen3.5-Omni backbone and English-only zero-shot evaluation of Nemotron provide complementary evidence. Across the tested Qwen budgets, AU gains are larger under stronger pruning, without inference-time mask switching.

title: Visualizing Joint Ranking Distributions in Network Meta-Analysis with Hammock Plots
summary: Treatment ranking provides a summary of the relative effectiveness of competing treatments and is a key output of network meta-analysis (NMA). Existing visualizations primarily summarize marginal ranking distributions or present individual treatment hierarchies with limited insight into uncertainty in the overall hierarchy. We introduce hammock plots as a visualization framework for the joint posterior distribution of treatment rankings. Although motivated by treatment ranking in NMA, the proposed framework is broadly applicable to any setting in which uncertainty in posterior rankings is of interest. Specifically, we develop separate hammock plots to display relationships between (a) adjacent treatments or (b) adjacent ranks. Using highlighting, we show how to assess posterior support for selected treatment hierarchies, to evaluate hierarchies identified by ranking metrics against the posterior distribution, and to examine uncertainty within selected regions of the treatment hierarchy. We apply the proposed visualizations to a thrombolytic treatment network, which revealed patterns in the posterior ranking distribution and the location of uncertainty in treatment hierarchies that were difficult to identify using existing ranking graphics. We also provide a web application to generate all of the proposed hammock plot variations for any data set.

title: Multimodal Ambivalence and Hesitancy Recognition with Bidirectional Audio--Text Cross-Attention
summary: Ambivalence and hesitancy (A/H) are subtle behavioural states that can be expressed through both what a person says and how it is spoken. This paper presents an audio--text framework for video-level A/H recognition. Full-video transcripts and speech waveforms are encoded using pre-trained multilingual BERT and wav2vec~2.0, respectively, and projected into a shared representation space. Two stacked bidirectional cross-attention blocks allow linguistic tokens to attend to acoustic frames and acoustic frames to attend to linguistic context without requiring explicit temporal alignment. The resulting sequences are aggregated through masked mean pooling and combined using concatenation, element-wise products, and absolute differences for binary classification. We evaluate the model on the subject-independent split of the Behavioural Ambivalence/Hesitancy (BAH) dataset. The proposed system achieves 72.19\% accuracy, 75.00\% precision, 81.13\% recall, 77.95\% A/H F1-score, and 70.16\% Macro-F1 on the test set. These results demonstrate the potential of jointly modelling linguistic and acoustic information for automatic A/H recognition.code at:https://github.com/DorriG/ECCV.

title: Codec-Compatible Learned Compression for 3D Gaussian Splatting
comment: Accepted at the IEEE International Conference on Visual Communications and Image Processing (VCIP 2026). 5 pages, 3 figures, and 1 table
summary: Video-based 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) compression methods provide a practical route by representing Gaussian attributes as 2D maps and coding them with standard video codecs. Among these maps, high-dimensional non-DC spherical harmonics (SH-AC) maps contain the largest number of channels and account for a dominant portion of the bitstream. However, their statistics differ substantially from those of natural images, and the nonlinear dependencies among SH-AC coefficients remain insufficiently exploited. To address these issues, we propose CCT-GS, a Codec-Compatible learned Transform framework for 3DGS compression. CCT-GS first learns a generalized SH-AC transform that captures cross-scene regularities and converts SH-AC maps into compact codec-friendly bottleneck maps. It further introduces LoRA-based scene adaptation to recover scene-specific appearance details with lightweight side information. Experiments on MPEG GSC sequences demonstrate that CCT-GS consistently outperforms representative video-based baselines, achieving an average BD-rate reduction of 51.30% over the video-based anchor.

title: Diffusion Score Estimation with Shallow Neural Networks: Regularity, Approximation, and Finite-Sample Rates
summary: We study the sample complexity of estimating Ornstein--Uhlenbeck diffusion scores in $\mathbb R^d$ using denoising score matching (DSM) with finite-width shallow ReLU networks, and its implications for reverse-process sampling. Under weak differentiability and polynomial-growth conditions on normalized derivatives of the initial density, we combine complementary estimates from the Gaussian transition kernel and the initial density to obtain explicit Sobolev bounds that are uniform in time on each fixed ball. Combining these bounds with existing shallow-network approximation theory gives explicit control of the approximation error and a sufficient path-norm budget. We then use truncation and localized Rademacher complexity to establish high-probability risk bounds for path-norm-constrained empirical DSM minimizers with unbounded inputs and labels. Under additional bounded-density and sub-Gaussian assumptions, suitable choices of network width and path-norm budget yield squared $L^2(P_t)$ score risk $\widetilde O(n^{-(d+3)/(2d+3)})$ at each fixed time $t>0$, where $n$ is the number of independent training samples and $P_t$ is the forward marginal. The nonasymptotic bounds retain explicit dependence on diffusion time and the regularity and tail parameters of the initial distribution. Aggregating the score errors over a time grid and applying existing sampling theory together with an early-stopping bound yields a high-probability total-variation error $\widetilde O(n^{-(d+3)/(4d+6)})$ between the generated and original data distributions under suitable sampling parameters. Here $\widetilde O$ suppresses logarithmic factors for fixed dimension, confidence level, and initial distribution.

title: Commanding at the Speed of Sound: Audio-Centric Referring Expression Segmentation for Aerial Scenes
summary: Referring expression segmentation (RES) aims to localize targets at the pixel level guided by human instructions. However, current models predominantly follow a text-centric paradigm that treats discrete text as the primary interaction medium for these human instructions. This assumption is especially limiting in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) applications, where rapid response, hands-free operation, and natural communication are often critical. In this paper, we reconstruct UAV referring expression segmentation through an audio-centric perspective. Grounded in information theory, we demonstrate that raw audio provides a higher upper bound for extracting rich semantic features than transcribed text. To achieve this, we construct an audio-driven UAV referring expression segmentation benchmark named Aerial-AudioRES by augmenting VisDrone with synthesized speech, forming "audio-text-image-mask" quadruples. Specifically, we employ an ambiguity filtering mechanism to ensure referential uniqueness, and incorporate eight distinct timbres alongside 4 realistic noises to simulate authentic environments. To drive the paradigm shift from text-centric to audio-centric, we propose the end-to-end Audio-centric Referring Expression Segmentation Network (ARES-Net). Distinct from discrete text-visual matching, our approach learns to establish a direct soft alignment between continuous acoustic manifolds and multi-scale visual representations. Comprehensive experiments show that our method obtains a peak accuracy of 64.23% in oIoU and demonstrates robust generalization on a collected real-human test set. Furthermore, it significantly reduces total inference latency to one-third of the text-based method. Our code is publicly available.

title: Toroidal-OAM Hybrid Beam for Divergence-Suppressed OAM Wireless Communication
summary: Orbital angular momentum (OAM) beams offer spatially independent multiplexing in wireless communications, but their donut-shaped intensity diverges with mode order, causing power capture loss at finite apertures and unequal link budgets. We propose a toroidal-OAM hybrid beam that combines the angular confinement and strong longitudinal electric field of toroidal electromagnetic pulses from a coaxial horn with a conventional OAM beam, lowering angular spread and producing non-zero on-axis intensity. A far-field model is built as a weighted superposition of OAM uniform circular array (UCA) radiation, a super-Gaussian toroidal angular envelope, and a zeroth-order Bessel longitudinal field, controlled by three dimensionless parameters (toroidal confinement, coupling strength, longitudinal coefficient) tied to measurable hardware. Numerical results at 3 GHz with a $5λ$ aperture show 12--41% divergence reduction for OAM modes $\ell = 1$--$4$, while modes $\ell \geq 5$ become fully center-peaked. The suppression ratio stays unchanged for fixed $kR$, $κ$, $α$, $β$, and $\ell$. Link evaluation shows 6.4--30.9 dB received SNR gain, over 108% extension in fixed-efficiency link-budget range, and up to five orders of magnitude reduction in multi-mode power imbalance. The central null is filled to 8--100% of the peak; the hybrid beam does not mix OAM modes, with intended-mode power fraction above $0.54$ where the ring is well-defined. OAM mode-division multiplexing capacity at $z=500λ$ shows up to $2.1\times$ ($107\%$) capacity enhancement. Full-wave simulation in ANSYS HFSS corroborates the model, confirming the hybrid launcher preserves the OAM vortex phase while reducing divergence compared with a UCA-only baseline. These findings establish toroidal beam engineering as a practical tool for OAM-based wireless links.

title: Inference for Directions in Canonical Correlation Analysis with Partially Paired Data
summary: Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) is a classical tool for learning linear associations between two data views, and inference on canonical directions is the key for interpreting their coefficients and detecting interesting relationships. We study the problem of hypothesis testing for canonical directions when paired observations are supplemented by unpaired observations of either view. The key challenge is to incorporate the additional marginal information while accounting for its dependence on the paired sample used to estimate the canonical directions. To address this issue, we propose coupled augmentation functions that jointly use the marginal information from both views and construct a one-step estimator based on the resulting corrections. Theoretically, we show that under the null, the proposed estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal even when dimension grows at the rate $d = o(n)$. This result provides a sign-invariant Wald test statistic for detecting important variables in canonical directions. Through numerical studies, we show that the proposed test statistic with semi-paired data improves upon inference using paired data.

title: Exploring Representation Autoencoders for Text-to-Audio Generation
summary: Representation autoencoders (RAE), created by pairing a frozen pretrained self-supervised learning (SSL) encoder with a trained decoder, have recently demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on image generation. Their use in the audio domain, however, remains limited: text-to-audio (TTA) models are typically trained in the latent space of dedicated autoencoders where the encoder and the decoder are trained jointly with reconstruction objectives. This paper presents a study on audio representation autoencoders (AuRA) and their applicability to general audio TTA. We train decoders for two pretrained SSL audio encoders and evaluate their reconstruction quality against autoencoders used by recent TTA systems. After obtaining decoders for the SSL representations, we also train rectified flow models in the SSL and baseline latent spaces to isolate the autoencoder's effect on generation. We find that generation in SSL spaces achieves comparable or superior performance to generation in the baseline spaces, despite differences in reconstruction performance. These results highlight that reconstruction quality alone is not a sufficient proxy for generative performance.

title: ShlokaDhara: A Multi-Speaker Sanskrit Speech Corpus for Learning Meter-Aware Prosody in Text-to-Recitation
summary: Sanskrit verse recitation is governed by $\textit{Chandas}$, a strict prosodic framework defined by rhythmic $\textit{Laghu}$ (light) and $\textit{Guru}$ (heavy) syllables. Because existing Sanskrit speech datasets prioritize ASR or conversational TTS, they lack the metrical fidelity required for authentic verse synthesis. We introduce $\textbf{\textit{ShlokaDhara}}$, a 43-hour, multi-speaker Sanskrit speech corpus capturing diverse meters, recitation styles, and melodic variations. We specifically focus on $\textit{Text-to-Recite}$, a synthesis task explicitly requiring both prosodic accuracy and metrical correctness. Benchmarking state-of-the-art TTS architectures via an automated UTMOS (neural MOS) predictor demonstrates that XTTS-v2 achieves the highest perceptual quality. We further validate the XTTS-v2 generated samples using two paradigms: subjective assessments by 16 Sanskrit experts and novel empirical metrics, specifically, syllable-level $\textit{Laghu-Guru}$ duration analysis to objectively quantify structural metrical awareness. Ultimately, this work establishes a robust dataset and evaluation benchmark for prosody-aware computational Sanskrit recitation. Generated Samples: https://shlokadhara.vercel.app/

title: A plug-in estimator of the non-iterative conditional expectation g-formula using long short-term memory models
summary: The non-iterative conditional expectation (NICE) plug-in estimator of the g-formula can be used to estimate the causal effects of sustained treatment strategies, even in the presence of treatment-confounder feedback, under the assumptions of exchangeability, positivity, and consistency. In practical applications, parametric models are commonly used to estimate the joint distribution of confounders, treatments, and outcomes over time. As an alternative to parametric models, long short-term memory (LSTM) models, designed to capture both short-term patterns and long-range dependencies in sequential data, may better accommodate complex temporal dependencies among time-varying confounders, treatments, and outcomes. However, the validity of statistical inferences of a plug-in estimator based on LSTM models has not yet been investigated. Here, we provide proof of principle that, under a complex data generation mechanism that resembles data from a cohort of persons with HIV and sufficiently large sample sizes, an LSTM-based NICE g-formula plug-in estimator results in less bias than parametric estimators while achieving near-nominal coverage for 95\% confidence intervals. This work is intended to spur the development of a theoretical framework that encompasses deep learning plug-in estimators for causal inference based on high-dimensional longitudinal data.

title: Navalia: Advancing Cowork Agents through Verifiable Task Synthesis and Long-Horizon Post-Training
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are evolving from conversational assistants into Cowork Agents capable of autonomous planning, tool use, and complex task execution. Financial analysis requires these agents to integrate cross-document evidence and perform multistep numerical reasoning, but expert task authoring is costly, while direct LLM synthesis struggles to produce challenging tasks with reliable answers. We introduce Navalia, a framework for Cowork Agents that combines verifiable task synthesis with long-horizon post-training. Using corporate financial reports as its data source, Navalia semantically selects supporting evidence from complete fact sets and constructs executable computation chains to generate analytical tasks with traceable evidence and actual data dependencies between steps. We further use independent LLM review and programmatic checks to verify evidence consistency and answer correctness. The verified tasks are then used for trajectory collection, cold-start supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL) to improve long-horizon task execution. Navalia, initialized from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, achieves consistent gains over the base model across all five benchmarks: OfficeQA Pro, FinSearchComp, Finance Agent Benchmark, APEX-Agents-AA, and Workspace-Bench-Lite. These results demonstrate that Navalia improves evidence integration, tool use, and long-horizon task execution capabilities and generalizes to broader Cowork settings, including general office tasks.

title: Point2Acoustic: Efficient Room Acoustic Parameter Estimation from 3D Geometry and Material Properties
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to IEEE ICASSP 2027
summary: Scene-adaptive immersive audio rendering requires rapid estimation of acoustic parameters that reflect the surrounding environment. For repeated runtime scene updates, performing a detailed geometric-acoustic simulation for every update can be computationally costly. We present Point2Acoustic, a learning-based framework for direct estimation of six-band reverberation time ($RT_{60}$) and reverberant-to-direct ratio (RDR) from 3D scene geometry and acoustic material properties. Each scene is represented by a surface-sampled point cloud with spatial coordinates and frequency-dependent absorption and scattering coefficients, and encoded using PointNet or PointNet++. We train and evaluate the framework on a synthetic furnished-room dataset with varied geometry and acoustic materials, using geometric-acoustic simulation to obtain reference targets. Point2Acoustic achieves accurate multi-band prediction with millisecond-scale inference, and ablation results indicate that explicit global room descriptors and semantic surface labels provide no consistent benefit. The proposed formulation supports efficient scene-adaptive acoustic rendering in extended reality (XR).

title: Doubly Robust Estimation and Inference for Longitudinal Win Probabilities with Ordinal Outcomes in Observational Studies
summary: Repeated ordinal outcomes capture how treatment benefits and harms evolve over time. We develop doubly robust estimation and inference for visit-specific win probabilities and their prespecified weighted summaries, with Desirability of Outcome Ranking as a motivating example. Baseline confounding is addressed through augmented inverse-probability weighting (AIPW) of treatment-specific marginal category probabilities or joint multinomial targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE). We consider fold-specific and pooled targeting and establish conditions for double-robust consistency and semiparametric efficiency under participant-level cross-fitting. When only one nuisance model is correctly specified, inference based only on the efficient influence function may be invalid. For smooth parametric nuisance models, we derive covariance corrections from the complete estimating procedure, including targeting. When a correctly specified propensity model is estimated by maximum likelihood, a simplified score correction accommodates convergent flexible outcome learners without requiring their derivatives. The corrected covariance estimators retain within-participant dependence and support visit-specific, weighted-summary, and joint inference across repeated assessments. Simulations supported double robustness, demonstrated the importance of cross-fitting with overfit learners, and showed improved marginal and joint confidence coverage with the proposed corrections. TMLE, particularly with pooled targeting, often had lower root mean squared error under adequate treatment overlap, whereas AIPW was more stable under weak overlap. An electronic health record study of hospitalized adults with an acute respiratory illness illustrates how the trajectory and weighted summary reveal complementary aspects of the treatment comparison.

title: Mixture of Phonetic Experts Based Low-Rank Adaptation of Conformer Models for Accented English Speech Recognition
comment: Accepted at Interspeech 2026 (Sydney, 27 September to 1 October 2026). 5 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables
summary: We present Mixture of Phonetic Experts based Low-Rank Adaptation (MoPE-LoRA), a parameter-efficient adaptation framework for accented English speech recognition. Recent mixture-of-experts approaches typically allocate experts per accent, implicitly treating accent identity as the primary axis of variation. In contrast, we organize adaptation along phonetic categories, motivated by the observation that accent differences are often expressed as systematic distortions of phoneme realization. MoPE-LoRA introduces a fixed set of six low-rank experts aligned with manner-of-articulation classes and performs frame-level routing through a hybrid mechanism that combines phoneme supervision with learned acoustic gating. Because the expert set is shared across accents, the model does not require accent-specific modules and naturally extends to previously unseen accents. Experiments on L2-ARCTIC show that MoPE-LoRA consistently improves over single LoRA and full fine-tuning. In zero-shot evaluation where one accent is held out during training, the proposed method yields a 12.3% relative improvement over single LoRA. These results indicate that phonetic-category-based decomposition offers a scalable and transferable alternative to accent-level adaptation.

title: Channel-Level Mask Guidance for Slimmable Image Compression
comment: 14 pages, 12 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems for Video Technology (TCSVT)
summary: Learned image compression (LIC) has achieved promising rate-distortion performance, but most methods lack scalability for diverse platforms with varying computational and storage constraints. Existing slimmable LIC methods achieve flexible complexity via consecutive-channel activation but suffer from two limitations: forced consecutive-channel selection degrades narrow-model performance at low bitrates, and the lack of stable variable-rate control limits adaptability to varying bandwidth. We propose a channel-level mask-guided slimmable image compression method. A learnable channel-wise mask with sparsity-promoting regularization enables non-contiguous top-w channel selection, letting narrow models use the most informative channels. After training, mask merging and channel reordering convert the model into a standard slimmable network via Mask-to-Slimmable (M2S) conversion, enabling efficient inference without architectural changes. For variable-rate control, we combine lambda- and width-conditioned modulation with quantization-step scaling and a progressive training pipeline stabilized by a freeze-then-fine-tune strategy. Experiments on Kodak across E2E, Hyperprior, and Checkerboard backbones show superior rate-distortion performance across widths and bitrates, with large gains for narrow models at low bitrates. At w=48, it achieves up to 19.22%, 24.11%, and 22.76% BD-rate savings over the same-width Slimmable baseline on E2E, Hyperprior, and CKBD, respectively. A single VBR model replaces 40 independent models, reducing storage by 14.8x to 15.9x. Code: https://github.com/sjtu-tcloud/MGSIC.

title: A copula-based competing risks model with application to cancer risk estimation in family studies
summary: Cancer risk estimation tools are used by clinicians to evaluate the risk of individuals who carry high-risk pathogenic variants. In this article, we propose a new competing risks model designed to provide personalized estimates of the risk of developing breast or ovarian cancer as the first event among women carrying pathogenic variants in the BRCA1 gene. Our approach incorporates both the personal and complete family history of cancer of these high-risk women and introduces some flexibly in the modeling of the dependence among members of the same family. We use a Gaussian copula with a correlation matrix expressed in terms of the kinship coefficients of pairs of members. Furthermore, we develop an iterative estimation algorithm to estimate the parameters of the underlying model in the presence of a selection bias inherent to the family recruitment process. The performance of the proposed method is evaluated through a simulation study. An application to the Breast Cancer Family Registry data highlights the ability of the model to provide personalized estimation of the risk of developing breast cancer or ovarian cancer as the first event within the competing risks framework.

title: Learning from Past Mistakes: AI-Assisted Analytics of Software Defects and Their Fixes for Future Defect Prevention - An Industrial Case Study
summary: Context. Despite advances in software testing and quality assurance, defects continue to recur in industrial software systems. Defect data are routinely collected in issue-tracking systems, but their use is largely confined to detection, reporting, and short-term resolution, leaving the knowledge embedded in historical defects and their fixes under-exploited for prevention and long-term improvement. Objective. This paper investigates how historical defect and defect-fix data can be analyzed, with AI assistance under human oversight, to identify the human-error origins of recurring defects and to feed that understanding back into prevention and QA improvement. Method. We developed an AI-assisted, human-in-the-loop analytics approach that classifies defects by failure type and by human-error origin across the SDLC, determines how each could have been prevented, and synthesizes engineer-focused capability-building insights. It was deployed and evaluated in a large software company through an industrial case study, using practitioner surveys and interviews, classification-reliability checks, and an effort-normalized analysis of defect density. Results. Practitioners and independent review judged the classifications accurate; the outputs were rated useful and actionable; and defect density decreased after the introduction of the feedback, a tentative association we interpret as consistent with, but not proof of, a positive effect, given the study's uncontrolled pre/post design. Conclusion. AI-assisted, human-governed analysis of defect-fix data can help shift organizations from defect detection toward prevention, continuous learning and improvement.

title: Dynamic Line Ratings Counteract Transmission Investment Needs Driven by Climate Change
comment: 16 pages, 7 figures, supplementary information included, under review at Energy & Environmental Science
summary: Rising temperatures due to climate change will reduce power system transmission capacity. This reduction will interact with an ongoing shift from static to time-varying transmission rating standards. Previous research has yet to disentangle the effects of changing rating standards and climates on investment decisions. We quantify transmission investment needs for the Western U.S. power system (WECC) through mid-century under climate change and three rating standards: static ratings (SLR), ambient-adjusted ratings (AAR), and dynamic line ratings (DLR). By embedding alternative rating standards and high-resolution future weather data into a generation and transmission expansion model, PyPSA-USA, we find WECC will lose 1-3% of its transmission capacity across potential future climates under static ratings by mid-century, necessitating a 1-5% increase in transmission investment. Adoption of AAR or DLR eliminates most (81-99%) of the adaptation-driven transmission capacity needs, and further reduces aggregate transmission investments (by up to 31%). Additionally, we demonstrate that planning with time-varying ratings does not increase investment variability for individual lines under climate uncertainty relative to planning with static ratings. Our results emphasize the value and practicality of considering alternative rating standards in climate adaptation planning.

title: Choose your own adventure: How data source selection shapes urban accessibility analyses
summary: Urban park accessibility shapes mental health, physical well-being, and community cohesion. Measuring it is thus central to urban and landscape planning. Although researchers have debated the impacts of different accessibility measures on analysis results, scant attention has been paid to variability from data source selection. Do the results of accessibility analyses vary depending on the dataset used to define park locations and attributes? We compare four widely used geospatial data sources - OpenStreetMap, Esri, SafeGraph, and The Trust for Public Land - by validating their data and measuring park access across two cities. These datasets purport to cover the same spatial features, but our findings reveal wide discrepancies in accessibility results, driven by differences in dataset completeness, coverage, and accuracy between the sources. We provide guidelines for selecting and carefully validating data for accessibility analyses, as these decisions directly impact the accuracy and equity of downstream urban park planning and decision-making.

title: TRACE: Trustworthy Reasoning from Acoustic Cues and Evidence
summary: We introduce TRACE (Trustworthy Reasoning from Acoustic Cues and Evidence), a benchmark for diagnosing the reliability of large audio-language models (LALMs) by revealing when, and under what acoustic conditions these models behave untrustworthily. Existing benchmarks primarily measure whether a model produces the correct answer, but correctness alone cannot determine whether the answer is grounded in acoustic evidence or instead reflects language and contextual priors. TRACE evaluates model behavior along three complementary dimensions: (1) task performance, whether the answer is correct; (2) evidence alignment, whether the model is attending to the audio regions required to answer the question; and (3) robustness, whether answers and attributed evidence respond coherently to controlled changes such as event order, overlap, signal-to-noise ratio, or background content. TRACE targets temporal ordering, counting, and event existence, three tasks that remain challenging for current models. We synthesize contextually informed acoustic scenes that allow us to test whether models hallucinate events associated with the context but absent from the audio. This synthesis also allows us to obtain a scalable benchmark for which we know the answers by design. For each scene, we create controlled variants in a programmatic way to stress-test model robustness. We introduce attribution-based metrics that quantify model attention at scale on target events and non-target events. Evaluation across five state-of-the-art models shows that current LALMs often detect where relevant sound evidence occurs, but they do not reliably interpret it, integrate it into the answer, or respond to controlled changes in that evidence. Our benchmark also shows that models still struggle the most with ordering and counting questions.

title: pyFDN: A Python Toolbox for Feedback Delay Network Design, Analysis, and Optimization
summary: Feedback delay networks (FDNs) provide a compact representation of recursive audio systems for artificial reverberation and decorrelation. Their practical use spans structured matrix design, acoustic decay shaping, numerical simulation, and modal analysis, increasingly combined with differentiable optimization. We present pyFDN, an open-source Python toolbox that brings these operations into a common workflow. The library combines numerical design and analysis routines with block-based time-domain processing and integration with FLAMO for frequency-domain differentiable processing. Explicit network builds and JSON presets connect design, optimization, rendering, and reuse. This paper describes the software architecture, representative capabilities, and reproducibility mechanisms of version 0.5.0, providing a reference for research and teaching that use the toolbox.

title: Communication Complexity of Universal Features
summary: Motivated by the notion of features from machine learning, we study the complexity of representing data that allows for evaluation with a given family of functions. Concretely, we consider a deterministic encoder that observes $X\sim D$ and produces a finite encoding before a task $f\in\mathcal{F}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathcal{X}}$ is specified. For each task, a decoder must predict $f(X)$ with error at most $\varepsilon$ under $D$. We construct an encoder that outputs a representation with $O(d^{*}\log(1/\varepsilon))$ bits, where $d^{*}$ is the dual VC dimension of $\mathcal{F}$. Our encoder greedily selects $O((d^{*}/\varepsilon)\log(1/\varepsilon))$ functions from the class and uses their joint label pattern to produce the encoding. The key idea in our upper bound is a novel potential function argument, where we compare the entropy gained from each greedy selection with the number of patterns allowed by the dual VC dimension. We present lower bounds showing that the representation length achieved by our encoder is worst-case optimal for every $d^* \ge 1$ and $\varepsilon < 1/4$ up to a universal constant factor, and instance-wise optimal for every family $\mathcal{F}$ up to an $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ factor. We give two ways to learn the representation from unlabeled samples, with different guarantees on the representation size and sample complexity. Experimentally, we verify the greedy construction's accuracy-size tradeoff and explore its connection to neural sparse autoencoders.

title: EGGHead: Efficient Generalizable Gaussian Heads from a Single Image
summary: Creating photorealistic human heads typically involves trade-offs between representation power, efficiency, and generalizability. Traditional mesh-based solutions relying on 3DMMs generally sacrifice representation power but are efficient to render. On the other hand, NeRF-based methods improve representation power and fidelity while sacrificing efficiency. Gaussian splatting methods attempt to resolve these trade-offs by offering both high representation power and efficiency with real-time rendering. However, their efficiency nonetheless depends on the number of rasterized Gaussians, and the time needed to optimize and prepare the head (the enrollment time) is often high. In light of this, we propose EGGHead, which introduces a novel Gaussian allocation algorithm that efficiently assigns Gaussians to the head's semantic regions given a fixed Gaussian budget. Our algorithm reduces the number of Gaussians needed while minimizing the impact on representation power. EGGHead operates in a single forward pass and outperforms previous single-image face modeling methods in reconstruction quality, novel view synthesis, and rendering speeds.

title: QoS-Aware Joint 1-Bit RIS Element Activation and Fluid-Antenna Port Selection
summary: This letter jointly optimizes fluid-antenna port selection, fixed-cardinality reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) element activation, and 1-bit reflection phases through an exact angular event sweep that extends full-activation divide-and-sort geometry to subset selection. We establish deterministic gain bounds and activation monotonicity, derive exact single-element outage expressions and high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) asymptotics for independent RIS branches with correlated receiving ports, and prove diversity order equal to the RIS element count for fixed positive-definite RIS covariance. With perfect instantaneous channel state information, a quality-of-service aware policy activates the minimum number of elements required to meet a target SNR while preserving full-activation outage probability. An explicit overhead condition identifies when reduced activation improves net energy efficiency. Correlated-channel benchmarks illustrate subset-selection gains, aperture effects, and overhead-dependent energy-efficiency tradeoffs.

title: Structural equation modelling--based meta-analytic model for diagnostic test accuracy studies
summary: Bivariate random-effects models are commonly used to jointly synthesize sensitivity and specificity in diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) meta-analysis. However, existing approaches may be sensitive to distributional assumptions and may produce biased estimates of accuracy and between-study heterogeneity with sparse meta-analytic data. We proposed a novel bivariate structural equation modelling (BSEM) approach for DTA meta-analysis and evaluated its performance relative to the bivariate linear mixed model (BLMM) and bivariate generalized linear mixed model (BGLMM). We conducted extensive simulations under varying study, sample-size, accuracy, and heterogeneity conditions. We assessed model performance using bias, root mean squared error (RMSE), confidence interval width, empirical 95% coverage probability (CP), and convergence. We generated study-specific random effects from bivariate normal, t, and Laplace distributions to assess robustness to distributional misspecification. We also applied the models to two empirical DTA datasets. The BSEM generally produced smaller bias and RMSE and nominal-level CP for pooled sensitivity and specificity than the BLMM, while the BGLMM generally yielded results between the two approaches. The BLMM showed stable convergence but tended to underestimate between-study heterogeneity. We observed similar performance patterns under the three random-effects distributions. In the empirical applications, differences between model estimates were generally consistent with patterns observed in the simulations. Overall, the proposed BSEM provided a flexible alternative approach for jointly modelling sensitivity and specificity in DTA meta-analysis, with performance that was generally favourable relative to the BLMM and comparable to the BGLMM across the simulated and empirical settings considered.

title: Large language model and reinforcement learning based autonomous construction and progress updates
summary: Due to the rapid growth of the global population, traditional construction methods are gradually unable to meet the current housing demand. The advancement of machine learning algorithms has encouraged researchers to explore their applications in the construction industry, leading to more intelligent and efficient building processes. In particular, the rise of large language models in recent years has provided more possibilities for the transformation from traditional construction to smart construction. In this study, a large language model and reinforcement learning based autonomous construction method is proposed. An enhanced soft actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithm is developed to plan actions for a mobile crane according to construction tasks. Robot kinematics and control algorithms are used to ensure that the actions generated by the reinforcement learning algorithm can be executed by the crane. In addition, a customized embedding model is developed to extract information from the construction environment according to user interests. Then, a large language model, ChatGPT 5, is used to update construction progress, provide safety information to control system, and generate construction progress reports. The feasibility of proposed method is verified through several full-scall retaining wall construction experiments.

title: Variational Blind Equalization for Dual-Polarization Free-Space Quantum Communications
summary: Dual-polarization free-space quantum communication links require receiver equalization under polarization mixing, fading, phase variation, and limited channel supervision. This paper investigates variational blind and semi-blind equalization using VISTA (Variational Inference for Signal Tracking and Adaptation), a variational autoencoder-based probabilistic physical parameter estimator. In the semi-blind branch, channel-relevant statistics are mapped to the underlying 2x2 complex polarization channel. We compare forward KL, reverse KL, Average Jeffreys, Max-KL, and Adaptive Jeffreys regularization and analyze directional KL asymmetry and the local effect of the regularization weight zeta. Over 500 paired Monte Carlo trials, forward KL is nearly insensitive to zeta, whereas reverse and symmetric objectives exhibit low-error regions followed by degradation under stronger regularization. At zeta = 3 x 10^-5, Average Jeffreys reduces median channel NRMSE by approximately 4.8% relative to forward KL at the same weight. Reduced KL asymmetry does not necessarily imply lower channel error. A separate fully blind QPSK receiver estimates a direct equalizer from received data only. Over 3000 paired trials, the VISTA variants have nearly identical median aligned block-NMSE, while their lower mean aligned block-NMSE relative to the CMA-plus-separation baseline is concentrated in difficult, large-error trials. Direct-W optimization with Adam reproduces most of this mean reduction. In the fully blind benchmark, the tested weak regularizers provide no resolved improvement over unregularized VISTA.

title: Mixture of Censored Partially Linear Experts Models for Symmetric or Asymmetric Data with or without Outlying Observations: A novel approach with two-piece scale-mixture of normal distributions
summary: Finite mixture of partially linear model and finite mixture of experts models offer flexible tools for analyzing heterogeneous data, especially when covariates influence subgroup structure. Partially linear models further enhance this flexibility by combining linear and nonlinear effects. In many applications, however, censoring and departures from normality complicate estimation. To address these issues, we introduce a semiparametric mixture of censored partially linear expert models based on the two-piece scale mixture of normal family, which can accommodate skewness, heavy tails, and censoring. The proposed framework enables closed-form expressions in the E-step of an ECME algorithm, avoiding MCMC-based approximations and yielding stable maximum likelihood estimates. Simulation studies and real data analyses demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in settings with both heterogeneity and censoring.

title: MOSS: A Production Framework for Monitoring and Diagnosing Semantic Failures in Search and Recommendation Systems
comment: 10 pages. A prior version of this work was presented at the non-archival Unified Search and Recommendation Workshop (USRW), co-located with ACM RecSys 2026. This manuscript is currently under review at IEEE BigData 2026
summary:
Detecting semantic failures in production recommendation and search systems is hard: behavioral metrics lag by days, manual review does not scale, and most LLM evaluation frameworks are designed for offline, fixed datasets rather than continuous operational monitoring. We present Model Sanity Service (MOSS), a production framework that addresses this operational gap by embedding LLM-based relevance scoring into a recurring monitoring loop with targeted sampling, strategy-aware prompting, structured alerting, and diagnostic follow-up prompting that categorizes failures into actionable root causes.
  MOSS has been running in production at a large U.S. retailer for over six months across recommendation, search, and offer surfaces, and has surfaced two confirmed serving defects. For one of these, a backfill blending defect, MOSS quantified the impact of the proposed fix offline as a 76.4\% relative reduction in alert rate. On a 498-pair human-annotated recommendation benchmark, frontier LLM judges achieve higher F1 and AUC point estimates than non-LLM baselines (internal production embeddings and SBERT), with the largest gains on strategy-dependent tasks requiring intent-level relational reasoning. The same judge, score scale, and threshold transfer to a 466-pair search benchmark spanning 21 queries with only a surface-specific prompt adaptation, achieving strong F1 and AUC without retuning. These results show that a single LLM monitoring framework can provide useful, actionable quality signals across multiple product discovery surfaces in a large-scale e-commerce setting.

title: Quaternion-Valued Adaptive Projection Statistics for Neural Receivers in Dual-Polarization Free-Space Quantum Communications
summary: Dual-polarization free-space quantum communication receivers produce two coupled complex heterodyne streams. We develop robust quaternion receiver methods for such links under fading, polarization mixing, calibration mismatch, impulsive contamination, and other non-Gaussian disturbances. The four polarization and quadrature components are encoded as quaternion-valued samples. We formulate an identifiable effective channel model, Quaternion-Valued Projection Statistics (QVPS), and Adaptive QVPS (AQVPS), which augments samplewise projection outlyingness with robust local second-order descriptors. Robust complex and quaternion channel estimators use radial Huber weighting, while QVPS and AQVPS are evaluated separately as disturbance diagnostics. Neural experiments compare matched real-, complex-, quaternion-, and widely linear complex-valued receivers. Robust estimation reduces sensitivity to non-Gaussian contamination. Local second-order descriptors improve detection of the tested localized disturbances relative to QVPS, and a descriptor-only ablation slightly outperforms full AQVPS. Complex LMMSE gives the lowest evaluation MSE in the clean Gaussian SNR sweep, whereas the Quaternion NN, among the compared receivers with their nominal activations, gives the lowest mean evaluation MSE in the tested contaminated sweeps. Activation-matched experiments indicate that much of the nominal Quaternion NN robustness is attributable to bounded activation rather than quaternion parameterization alone. The methods are evaluated at the receiver processing level and do not constitute a composable CV-QKD security proof.

title: A Bayesian machine learning approach to direct and spillover effects in cluster-randomized trials with noncompliance
summary: We develop a Bayesian machine learning approach for estimating direct and spillover effects in cluster-randomized trials with treatment noncompliance. To flexibly model outcomes and treatment receipt while accounting for within-cluster dependence, we combine Bayesian additive regression trees with cluster-level random effects. We augment the outcome regression with a peer-treatment clever covariate, defined as the predicted mean proportion of treated peers from a preliminary receipt model, to mitigate regularization-induced distortion of the effect decomposition. Within a Bayesian g-computation framework, we estimate cluster-average intent-to-treat effects and cluster-average local average treatment effects and examine sensitivity to the cross-world restrictions underlying their decomposition. Simulation studies show reduced bias under model misspecification, while the correctly specified parametric models show expected frequentist properties. We find that the clever covariate improves the decomposition of the total effect into direct and spillover components under moderate or strong spillover, with similar gains in smaller clusters. Its benefits vary with spillover strength, and the $95\%$ credible intervals remain conservative. An application to the Primary School Deworming Project in Kenya suggests reduced infection risk, with a larger estimated contribution from individual treatment receipt than from peer receipt. Overall, our approach provides a flexible Bayesian estimation of direct and spillover effect decomposition in the presence of treatment noncompliance.

title: Beckmann World Models: Direct Terminal-Map Learning for One-Step Action-Conditioned Prediction
summary: Action-conditioned world models support planning and policy evaluation by predicting future states. However, learning an accurate one-step predictor can require substantial training computation. We introduce Beckmann World Models (BWM), which learn a direct map from noise, visual history, and actions to future frames without a pretrained generative teacher. We adapt the terminal-map conservation law of Beckmann Transport Models to action-conditioned video prediction, training directly from noise-data pairs without conditional populations of generated samples required by DriftWorld. However, transport consistency on interpolated inputs does not ensure accurate prediction from the pure noise used at inference. We address this gap with endpoint-aligned training that directly supervises the source prediction, emphasizes motion and spatial structure, and teaches recovery from generated histories. All components train the same map and retain one network call per future chunk. On PushT and Robomimic Can, the final model reduces 64-frame prediction MSE by 68% and 57%, respectively, relative to same-backbone regression baseline. For policy evaluation, BWM achieves the lowest mean IoU error among the evaluated models, 0.0100, at 24.8 ms per four-frame PushT prediction. On Robomimic Can, the BWM stage trained with motion supervision and generated histories achieves 3.3 times higher throughput and 78% lower peak memory than local one-step DriftWorld. In a latent-space extension to RT-1 and Bridge-V2, equal-update controls show that feature supervision under generated histories improves perceptual prediction. These findings show how terminal-map learning can combine efficient training with accurate one-step visual prediction.

title: Multiplexed Label-Free Cytokine Sensing Using a 128x128 CMOS ISFET Array with Flexdym Microfluidic Partitioning
summary: Cytokine-mediated inflammation disorders such as sepsis and cytokine release syndrome demand bedside multiplex panels that resolve pro- and anti-inflammatory dynamics in minutes, yet label-free FET cytokine sensors remain limited to few devices, single analytes, and PDMS packaging that sorbs small molecules and leaches oligomers. We present a CMOS platform pairing a 128 x 128 ion-sensitive field-effect transistor (ISFET) array (SkyWater 130 nm, SiN gate) with a FlexDym 4 x 1 micro-well overlay that partitions the membrane into four chemically independent regions (approximately 2,176 pixels each, square-root-of-N averaging). Two wells carry capture antibodies (anti-IL-6, anti-IL-10), one is a non-specific reference, and one tests specificity; the transduced signal is defined as the differential current relative to the reference signal (Delta I_D(W_n) - Delta I_D(W_3)). Single-analyte dose-response measurements spanning 100 fM to 10 nM successfully resolve both IL-6 and IL-10 above the non-specific detection floor, including at healthy-serum baseline concentrations. The array shows a per-pixel pH sensitivity of 1.13 microamperes per pH unit (CV approximately 14%). Across two chips, device-to-device variation is dominated by transconductance spread (g_m CV approximately 62%); a one-time per-device g_m calibration reduces analyte-measurement variance to approximately 16%. We further validate the surface functionalization, characterize device-to-device variation, and demonstrate the FlexDym integration workflow. Simultaneous multiplexed cytokine measurements resolve IL-6 (W1) and IL-10 (W2) against the chemistry-only reference (W3). At the same time, cross-specificity characterization is assessed by applying IL-6 to an anti-IL-10 well (W4), establishing a scalable label-free ISFET architecture for multiplexed cytokine sensing.

title: Beyond exponential tilting: sharp asymptotics and improved importance sampling for rare events
summary: A classical approach for importance sampling (IS) of a rare event is to tilt the measure using its large deviation minimizer, thereby shifting the proposal mean towards the event set. While this tilt is log-efficient, we show that the coefficient of variation of the resulting estimator still grows like $\varepsilon^{-1/4}$ in the small-noise limit $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Motivated by sharp large deviation asymptotics and the local geometry of the event set at the minimizer, we propose improvements using a control variate or an anisotropic, non-Gaussian proposal. We prove, up to truncations that hold with high probability, and confirm empirically in high-dimensional examples, that the former bounds the coefficient of variation and the latter makes it vanish, so that a bounded number of samples suffices. Our analysis addresses both the coefficient of variation of the different proposals and their necessary and sufficient sample size based on the Kullback--Leibler divergence of the IS target from the proposal; both yield the same rates in $\varepsilon$. We demonstrate the resulting samplers, including a variant that blends the classical and the new proposal across noise levels, for a stochastic Korteweg--de Vries equation with thousands of random inputs.

title: Pareto-Optimal RTL Code Generation via Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning with Large Language Models
summary: Recent studies have proposed reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) methods that enable LLMs to generate high-quality RTL circuits from natural-language specifications. Existing approaches optimize circuit PPA (Power, Performance, Area) by aggregating multiple objectives into a single scalar reward, making it difficult to simultaneously generate diverse Pareto-optimal solutions across different trade-offs such as low power, low latency, and small area. However, in practical design, the relative importance of each objective varies depending on product requirements and design constraints; thus, obtaining a diverse and high-quality candidate set is beneficial in that designers can choose a preferred trade-off a posteriori. In this work, we are the first to propose a learning method for LLM-based circuit generation that optimizes, not the quality of a single circuit, but the quality and diversity of the entire circuit set obtained through multiple generations in the PPA objective space. The proposed method consists of (1) a generation-based training pipeline that reformulates coverage improvement of the entire Pareto solution set into a sequential circuit generation problem, and (2) a reward function based on Hypervolume Contribution (HVC) that measures how much a generated circuit contributes to the Pareto front. Evaluation on the RTLLM v2 benchmark shows that the proposed method achieves +13.3 percentage points in relative Hypervolume over a baseline without PPA optimization and +14.4 percentage points over a single-objective reinforcement learning method, while also demonstrating superiority in circuit diversity.

title: Structured PARAFAC Channel Estimation for Flexible Intelligent Metasurface Receivers
summary: Flexible intelligent metasurfaces (FIMs) create geometric diversity through aperture morphing, but their configuration-dependent responses complicate uplink channel estimation. This letter considers multiple users sharing a common angular response and develops a structured PARAFAC model across calibrated FIM configurations. Its known identity factor and rank-one pilot-weighted channel factor enable deterministic, noniterative algebraic factor recovery through per-element rank-one approximations, reference-state normalization, global rank-one projection, and a least-squares morphing-factor update. The recovered spatial and morphing factors are then jointly matched to the calibrated manifold to estimate the common angles, user gains, and configuration-dependent channels. Simulations demonstrate accurate recovery and show that out-of-plane morphing resolves the azimuth-sign ambiguity of an undeformed planar aperture; an angular-spread experiment quantifies the mismatch when the common-response assumption is relaxed.

title: Geometry-informed importance sampling for rare events
summary: We propose GeoIS, a new importance sampling method for estimating rare event probabilities for an underlying Gaussian distribution that exploits asymptotic theory and local event geometry. The proposal distribution is a mixture of two components. The first component draws a Gaussian along the boundary near the instanton and adds to it an exponentially distributed shift into the rare event. This component is derived from the known asymptotic approximation to the optimal zero-variance proposal distribution. The second mixture component is designed to cover missing event mass due to boundary-approximation mismatch, thereby preserving unbiasedness. We rigorously analyze this sampling strategy's performance as a function of event geometry, dimension, rarity level, and number $N$ of importance samples. Under explicit and relatively mild conditions on the former three features, we prove that the squared relative error of GeoIS is bounded by $c/N$ with high probability, for an absolute constant $c$. We implement our method numerically in several examples, including a diffusion PDE problem. The numerical experiments exhibit the qualitative dependence on geometry, dimension, rarity and sample size predicted by the theory, and show that GeoIS markedly outperforms importance sampling methods that use a fully Gaussian proposal distribution.

title: InterType: Breaking the Single-Function Barrier in Neural Binary Type Inference
summary: Variable type recovery is a critical task in binary reverse engineering, enabling downstream applications such as vulnerability discovery, malware analysis, and security enforcement. While recent Transformer-based models have demonstrated strong performance in type inference by learning instruction-level semantics, they predominantly operate within single-function boundaries (i.e. intra-procedural analysis), ignoring the rich type constraints that propagate across function calls. Empirical studies have shown that nearly 44% of variables in real-world binaries propagate across function boundaries as arguments or return values, representing a significant source of type information that intra-procedural models cannot exploit. In this paper, we propose InterType, a method that embeds inter-procedural analysis into a pre-trained Transformer model for binary type recovery. Our approach builds on CodeArt, a state-of-the-art Transformer model for stripped binary analysis, and extends it by incorporating caller-callee data flow dependencies during fine-tuning. Specifically, we extract data flow dependence for each caller-callee pair from disassembled binaries and construct training instances that provide the model with cross-function context. By exposing the Transformer to inter-procedural variable propagation patterns, our model learns to resolve types that depend on cross-function data flow. We evaluate InterType on the coreutils benchmark compiled with optimization levels O0 through O3. On O1 binaries, InterType improves recall by 2.76 percentage points, from 89.00% for the intra-procedural CodeArt baseline to 91.76%, corresponding to a 25.1% reduction in recall error rate (1 - recall).

title: RealComm: Benchmarking and Adapting Audio Deepfake Detection over Real Communication Channels
comment: 12 pages, 9 figures, and 3 tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Audio, Speech and Language Processing
summary: Acoustic capture, device processing, and transmission coding in real calls jointly alter speech signals and may affect the reliability of audio deepfake detection. To systematically evaluate these effects, we introduce RealComm, a dataset pairing digital speech with recordings of the same utterances transmitted through real mobile calls. The acquisition design covers acoustic and wired injection, handset and speakerphone operation, and caller-side denoising, with bona fide and synthetic speech recorded under matched conditions. The dataset includes RealCommBench for evaluation and RealCommTrain for adaptation. We further develop RealComm-Aug, a staged waveform augmentation pipeline for simulating acquisition and transmission effects, and investigate its combination with real-call training. Experiments with existing detectors reveal substantial degradation after call transmission, even for models with strong digital-domain performance; acoustic injection is particularly challenging. Paired quality and spectral analyses show that quality degradation is associated with poorer detection across recording conditions for the evaluated detectors, while high-frequency attenuation alone does not explain detection difficulty. Simulated augmentation and real-call training provide complementary benefits, with their combination achieving the lowest call-domain error for each of three evaluated detectors. For Teffic-Audio, the equal error rate decreases from 37.94% to 22.37%. The demo and benchmark access information are provided through the project repository.

title: Beyond Scalar Leaderboards: Adaptive Sampling for Pareto Frontier Identification in Multi-Objective LLM Arenas
summary: The evaluation of large language models (LLMs) is inherently multi-objective, as different models may offer different tradeoffs across performance dimensions such as math, code, and writing. Because such evaluations are often based on costly and time-consuming human feedback, it is important to draw reliable conclusions using as few comparisons as possible. In this paper, we present Vector-Borda Empirical-Gap Elimination (VB-EGE), a fixed-confidence adaptive sampling algorithm for efficiently identifying models on the Pareto frontier in arena-style evaluation, where each comparison evaluates a pair of models on a prompt with respect to a selected performance dimension. VB-EGE progressively eliminates models from an active set once sufficient statistical evidence has been accumulated to certify their Pareto status. Under a multi-objective Bradley-Terry model, we show that VB-EGE returns the correct Pareto frontier with high probability and derive an instance-dependent upper bound on its sample complexity. We further establish a worst-case lower bound showing that VB-EGE is minimax-optimal up to logarithmic factors. Simulations and experiments on three real-world Arena datasets (Arena, SearchArena, and VisionArena) demonstrate VB-EGE's empirical effectiveness.

title: Uncertainty Gates the Gradient: Adaptive Updates for Generalized Few-Shot 3D Segmentation
summary: In generalized few-shot 3D point cloud segmentation, support annotations are often compromised by sparsity and occlusion. Blindly adapting to such low quality samples risks learning spurious geometric patterns rather than robust novel concepts. Although 3D Vision-Language Models have been introduced to sup plement supervision, the potential of uncertainty to actively govern adaptation dynamics remains underexplored. Existing signal-level methods like loss reweight ing fail to prevent unreliable episodes from steering the optimization trajectory. To address this, we propose Uncertainty-Gated Adaptive (UGA), to the best of our knowledge the first framework that elevates uncertainty to update-level gating for generalized few-shot 3D point cloud segmentation. The core mod ule, Uncertainty-Gated Update (UG-Update), estimates episodic reliability via intra-class dispersion over merged support and pseudo-labeled novel supervision, and selectively gates residual gradient updates. This encourages the model to learn novel semantics from reliable episodes while attenuating updates during unreliable ones.
